newsitem.title: USA: NYC Mayor to study first hospital privatizations.
newsitem.headline: NYC Mayor to study first hospital privatizations.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who on Thursday heralded his administration's success in turning around public hospitals, said whether or not more than three hospitals would be privatized depended on the results.
"What I have always said is you do the first one, and then you do the next two, and then you see how they work," said Giuliani at a news conference at Bellevue Hospital Center.

The Giuliani Administration's plans to privatize three hospitals were derailed in January, when a New York State Supreme Court Judge ruled it must get the City Council's approval. Council leaders have opposed the mayor's plans and Giuliani two weeks ago appealed the court's ruling, which stalled a plan to lease Coney Island Hospital in Brooklyn to PHS New York. The mayor also was seeking bidders for the Elmhurst and Queens Hospital Centers in Queens.
Asked why privatization was needed if the city's hospitals performance had improved, Giuliani explained that having an alternative helped push the public system to do better.
"I'm not ideologically totally commited to pritatization, I'm not ideologically totally commited to government ownership of things. I think there needs to be a balance between the two," he said.
The mayor displayed a number of charts that showed just how far the city's hospitals had come since fiscal 1991 to 1993, when accreditation was conditional or delayed for six hospitals.

All 11 got immediate, three-year accreditation in fiscal 1994 to 1996, he said, presenting charts that showed the city had begun turning around problems, like the heavy reliance on emergency rooms, whose use had dropped 7.1 percent by fiscal 1996, when measured against fiscal 1993.
Rick Langfelder, chief financial officer for the Health and Hospitals Corp, said the data for the first six months of fiscal 1997 indicated the same postive trends had continued.

Giuliani noted the public hospitals have agreed new, performance-based contracts with private affiliates, which, for example, will measure if 100 percent of emergency room consultations are done within 30 minutes by a privileged doctor. But he was frank about the need for more improvements.
"This was a system that was in grave jeopardy of being perceived as a failure," he said.
"This is a good step, a good step in the right direction...This is hardly the be all and the end all, but this is a good beginning and a solid base on which to build."
